text: Infertility (a sow's inability to produce piglets) has several distinct patterns. Anoestrus: the normal cycle is about 21 days (18–24 days range), with estrus expected at 6 months in gilts and 5–7 days after weaning in sows — when it fails to appear, mating/insemination becomes impossible. Causes: poor body condition at weaning (from underfeeding during lactation, or a painful leg preventing normal eating) — recovery takes a while, so better feed management during lactation prevents this; improper estrus detection (crossbred pigs, especially gilts, can show only subtle vulva swelling/reddening and little behavioral change — careful daily observation and checking for immobility is needed; gilts are typically mated at their 3rd estrus, around 8 months); improper technique to induce estrus (stress, light, boar stimulus, and extra feeding are all needed — a quiet, dark environment with no boar and restricted diet suppresses estrus); and ovarian cysts (multiple cysts cause prolonged anoestrus, though this accounts for under 10% of anoestrus cases). Repeat breeding: estrus reappears weeks after mating/AI — 'regular' repeat breeding recurs about 21 days (18–22 days) after the previous estrus. Causes: generalized disease (PRRS is now a common cause, along with other reproductive failures, abortion, stillbirths, weak newborns — repeat breeding here is irregular, 21–35 days after mating); endometritis (uterine inflammation/infection prevents placental development and embryo survival, terminating the pregnancy — animals often look clinically normal apart from mild vaginal discharge; caused mainly by E. coli, Staphylococcus, or Streptococcus entering the uterus after farrowing or during estrus; treat with Tetracycline, Amoxicillin, or TMP+Sulfa mixed in feed for 1 week starting on the first day of estrus). Boar infertility: a boar can look healthy with good-condition testicles but still produce poor-quality semen — common causes are overuse (mating/collection should not exceed 3 times/week, or spermatozoid concentration drops sharply) and fever (testicles need a cooler-than-body temperature to produce sperm — an animal with fever above 40°C can become sterile for about 3 weeks even after it has otherwise recovered).
